title: Poster mechanisms — Image Wiki
text:
Poster mechanisms
  The named moves a poster can make on a passer-by — fourteen of them, several arranged as deliberate opposites — and why they are moves rather than styles.

  
    Termposter mechanisms
    Also calledposter devices, how posters work, poster rhetoric
    Not the same asposter styles, advertising copy, visual hierarchy
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The fourteen mechanismsWhy several of them are oppositesReading the mechanism off a real posterCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  You pass a poster at walking speed. It gets about one second, from four or five metres away, competing with traffic and your phone. If something in it catches, you slow down and give it maybe ten seconds more, from arm's length.
Nearly every poster that has ever worked was built for those two moments. The first one decides whether the second one happens. So a poster is not one picture — it is two, stacked in the same rectangle, and most of what looks like style in poster design is really a way of arranging that pair.
Cooper Hewitt's 2015 exhibition How Posters Work, curated by Ellen Lupton, put the point bluntly by refusing to organise its 125 posters by country, period or movement. It sorted them into fourteen mechanisms instead — fourteen things a designer can do to your eye. That is the taxonomy this article uses, and it is worth learning because it gives you something to say about a poster other than which decade it came from.


Focus the eye: Flagg, 1917
Overwhelm the eye: Strobridge Litho. Co., 1899


Two mechanisms that Cooper Hewitt lists as neighbours and opposites. Both public domain.
Left, James Montgomery Flagg, I Want You for U.S. Army, 1917. One head, dead centre, filling two thirds of the sheet, with a pointing fist thrust forward at you and four words underneath. There is nothing else in the frame to look at. That is focus the eye.
Right, The Barnum & Bailey Greatest Show on Earth, printed by the Strobridge Lithographing Company, 1899. Count the things competing for you: twelve tents, thirty-odd flags, a locomotive, seven wagons, a crowd, two bands of shouting type. Your eye starts a tour and never settles. That is overwhelm the eye, and for a circus it is the honest answer — the promise is abundance, so the poster is made of abundance.


The fourteen mechanisms
Cooper Hewitt's list, with the shortest gloss I can give each:

Focus the eye — one thing, big, usually near the middle.
Overwhelm the eye — dense pattern and competing colour, so the eye wanders.
Use text as image — letters doing the picture's job, not just labelling it.
Overlap — one shape in front of another, the cheapest depth cue there is.
Cut and paste — fragments of photographs recombined into a new claim.
Assault the surface — the image bent, burnt, torn, defaced, scribbled over.
Simplify — remove until only the load-bearing shape is left.
Tell a story — a moment that makes you ask what happened, or what happens next.
Amplify — shouting, in image or in type: screaming mouths, all caps.
Double the meaning — one image that reads two ways at once.
Manipulate scale — things sized wrongly on purpose.
Activate the diagonal — a slanted axis that cuts across the rectangle.
Make eye contact — a face that looks back at you.
Make a system — a kit of colours and forms that survives being reused.


OPEN AIRunreadablestill readsThe first read3 m away, about one secondOPEN AIRSaturday 14 June, gates from 6 pmRiverside Park, north entranceSix stages, one ticket, no glassUnder twelves free with an adultLast train back leaves at 01.10readableThe second read1 m away, maybe ten seconds

The same design, twice, differing only in how far away you are standing. The eye resolves about one arcminute of detail, which is roughly 0.9 mm at 3 m and 0.3 mm at 1 m — so the small print is not small at 3 m, it is absent.
Left, the first read: one dark shape and two words. That is the whole message a passer-by receives, and it has to be enough to justify stopping. Right, the second read, where the times, the address and the price finally exist. Both reads are the poster's job; they are just not the same job.


Why several of them are opposites
Focus the eye and overwhelm the eye contradict each other. So do simplify and assault the surface. A taxonomy of virtues could not contain both halves of those pairs — which is the tell that these are not virtues. They are tools with jobs.
Simplify wins when the first read has to survive a hostile distance and the message is one idea. Overwhelm wins when the subject is abundance, or when you want the poster to be a thing people stand in front of rather than glance at: 1960s psychedelic concert posters are close to unreadable from across a street, on purpose, because their audience was already interested and already close.
So the useful question about a poster is never "is it too busy?" It is "busy for whom, at what distance, with how many seconds?"



El Lissitzky, Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge, 1919. Public domain.
Four mechanisms in one sheet, and you can point at each. Activate the diagonal: the wedge runs corner to corner, so the eye crosses the whole surface instead of resting in the middle. Simplify: two shapes, three colours, no drawing. Manipulate scale: the wedge and circle are enormous, the scattered bars tiny, and that size gap alone reads as force meeting mass.
And use text as image — the words are not a caption sitting under a picture. Each phrase is placed inside the shape it describes, the red words on the red side, the white words inside the circle, so the sentence and the diagram are the same object. Note what is not here: no face, no story, no eye contact. Those mechanisms were available and were declined.


Reading the mechanism off a real poster

Where did your eye land first, and was there competition? One landing site means focus; a tour means overwhelm. This is the Visual hierarchy question, asked of a sheet with one second to live.
Is there a face, and is it looking at you? Eye contact is the strongest pull in the set and the easiest to spot.
Is the main axis upright or slanted? A diagonal is a decision, never an accident.
Could you describe the image in one shape? If yes, someone simplified.
Is there a second meaning that arrives late? Doubling is the mechanism you notice on the second read, not the first.
Does the sheet look damaged on purpose? Torn, burnt, overprinted, sprayed: assault the surface.




Savile Lumley, Daddy, what did YOU do in the Great War?, published by the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee, 1915. Public domain.
Tell a story, run all the way. Nothing in this poster is dramatic: a patterned curtain, a green armchair, a girl with a picture book on her father's knee, a small boy on the carpet lining up toy soldiers and a toy field gun. The work is done by a question in the title and a gaze — the father is the only figure who is not looking at the book, and he is not looking at you either. He stares past the edge of the frame with his knuckles at his mouth.
That combination sets a time bomb: the scene is the future, the question has already been asked, and you supply the answer. Compare it with the Flagg poster above. Same war, same purpose, opposite mechanism — and note the cost. This one has no first read at all. From across a street it is a brown domestic interior with a line of script along the bottom.


Common mistakes

"These are styles." They are not. One poster usually runs three or four mechanisms at once, and the same mechanism turns up in Art Nouveau, Soviet constructivism and Swiss modernism alike. Style tells you where a poster came from; mechanism tells you what it does.
"Busy is bad." Busy is bad at three metres with one second. The Barnum sheet was pasted in rows on a hoarding people walked up to and read like a menu.
"The typography is the words and the image is the picture." In use text as image the letters are the picture. Judging the type as if it were only a label misses the whole design.
"Simplify means minimal." Simplify means removing what does not carry the message — usually reducing the sheet to a few flat areas of clearly different value. A simplified poster can still be loud, ugly and crowded with colour.
Confusing a mechanism with a subject. A screaming mouth is not the mechanism; amplify is, and it can also be done with capital letters, saturated red or a doubled exclamation.


Naming what a poster is doing, in twenty seconds

Stand back, or shrink it in your browser. What is the first read — one shape, one face, one word, or nothing?
Name the mechanism that produced that first read.
Come close. What arrives on the second read that you could not have had before?
Look for the opposite: which mechanism was clearly available and refused?
Ask who the poster was for and how close they were standing. Most "bad poster" judgements are really distance judgements.
